quote: Was die wichtige Frage der simultanen Annäherung 2er Funktionen {+$\varphi(x)$, $\psi(x)$+} durch rationale Funktionen mit dem- selben Nenner betrifft, so kommt dieselbe auf die Auffin- dung von 3 [-...-] ganzen Funktionen $P, Q, R$ hinaus
english: As for the important question of the simultaneous approximation of two functions φ(x), ψ(x) by rational functions with the same denominator, it amounts to finding three entire functions P, Q, R such that A ≡ Pφ + Qψ + R = x^N + ..., where N is as large as possible.
topic: Hilbert considers orthogonality properties of polynomials P_n with a weight factor (ξ−α), plans to find a second-order differential equation for them, and reduces simultaneous rational approximation of two functions to finding three polynomials P, Q, R.

triage.modern_statement: Given two functions φ, ψ (power series or functions analytic at a point, written here near x=0), find polynomials P, Q, R of prescribed degrees, not all zero, such that the linear form Pφ + Qψ + R vanishes to the highest possible order N (equivalently A = x^N + ...). This is Hermite–Padé approximation of type I (the 'Latin' problem) for the system (1, φ, ψ). Its dual, type II, is simultaneous rational approximation of φ and ψ by rational functions with a common denominator. For Markov/Stieltjes-type functions, the denominators are multiple orthogonal polynomials, which fits the orthogonality-with-weight context on the same page.
triage.answered_by: Hilbert did not originate this problem. Hermite introduced simultaneous rational approximation in his 1873 proof that e is transcendental, and Padé developed it further. Kurt Mahler began the formal general theory, culminating in 'Perfect systems' (Compositio Math. 19, 1968, 95–166); his students, Coates and Jager among them, contributed too. Later work by Angelesco, Nikishin, Gonchar, Rakhmanov, Aptekarev, Van Assche, López Lagomasino and others built the theory of multiple orthogonal polynomials and the asymptotics of Hermite–Padé approximants. The basic existence question is answered by linear algebra. Hilbert's note is not one of his 23 problems or the 24th problem.

evidence.claim: In 1873 Hermite proved e transcendental using simultaneous rational approximation of systems of exponentials. The formal theory of simultaneous rational approximation for general systems of analytic functions developed later.
Hermite introduced Hermite–Padé approximation. Mahler began the formal study for general systems of functions, with further papers by his students such as Coates.
Reference: K. Mahler, Perfect systems, Compositio Math. 19 (1968) 95–166.

Hermite–Padé approximation comes in two types. Type I asks for polynomial coefficients making a linear form in (f1,...,fr) vanish to high order. Type II is simultaneous approximation with a common denominator, and the denominators are orthogonal polynomials.
Multiple orthogonal polynomials are closely tied to Hermite–Padé approximants and are often called Hermite–Padé polynomials.
Research continues: for example, a 2024 arXiv paper on strong asymptotics of multiple orthogonal polynomials for Angelesco systems.

triage.why: Finding P, Q, R with Pφ + Qψ + R = x^N + ... and N as large as possible is exactly the textbook definition of type I Hermite–Padé approximation for (1, φ, ψ). Its dual (type II) is the common-denominator simultaneous approximation Hilbert mentions. The problem was introduced by Hermite in 1873 and systematized by Mahler (Perfect systems, 1968). It grew into the large field of Hermite–Padé approximation and multiple orthogonal polynomials, which is still active, for example in work on Angelesco and Nikishin systems and integrable systems. The general framework is solved and well known, but these sources do not show whether Hilbert's private note directly influenced any of this work. The note is not among Hilbert's published problems.
